items.prompt: Where should the colon go? You will need three things scissors, glue and paper.

options.text: after need
options.why: The colon comes before the list, not in the middle of the main clause.

options.text: after things
after scissors
options.why: Scissors is the first item in the list.

options.text: after glue
options.why: Glue is in the middle of the list.

hints: A colon can introduce a list.
The colon goes after a complete clause, just before the list starts.
Find the first item in the list. What comes just before it?
items.explanation: The colon introduces the list: You will need three things: scissors, glue and paper.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?

options.text: The rain; stopped the children ran outside.
options.why: A semicolon must come between two complete clauses.

options.text: The rain stopped; the children ran outside to play.
The rain stopped the children; ran outside.
options.why: The semicolon splits the second clause in the wrong place.

options.text: We bought; mangoes, bananas and papayas.
options.why: No punctuation is needed after bought.

hints: A semicolon joins two complete clauses that are closely linked.
Each side of the semicolon must make sense as a sentence on its own.
Cover the words after the semicolon. Does the first part make sense alone?
items.explanation: The rain stopped and the children ran outside to play are both complete clauses, and they are closely linked, so a semicolon can join them.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences where the colon is used correctly.

options.text: There is one rule in the library: whisper.
Pack these items: a torch, a map and a water bottle.
My favourite: fruit is mango.
options.why: The colon splits favourite fruit, which belong together.

options.text: We went: to the market.
options.why: The colon breaks up the sentence for no reason.

options.text: She: smiled at me.
options.why: The colon separates the subject from its verb.

hints: A colon comes after a complete clause.
A colon introduces something: a list, an explanation or an example.
Cover everything after each colon. Is the first part a complete clause?
items.explanation: In the correct sentences, a complete clause comes before the colon, and the colon introduces a rule or a list.

items.prompt: A semicolon is missing. Write the word that should come straight after it. Rani loves maths her brother prefers art.
hints: There are two complete clauses joined together with no punctuation.
Find where the first clause ends.
Who loves maths? Where does that idea finish?
items.explanation: The semicolon separates the two clauses: Rani loves maths; her brother prefers art.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences by the punctuation mark that belongs in the gap.

items.text: Ayu sang ___ Dewi played the flute.
Bring two things ___ a hat and water.
Bats fly at night ___ birds fly by day.
There is one problem ___ the rain.
The sun set ___ the sky turned orange.

hints: Look at the words after each gap.
If they are a list or a single idea that explains, use a colon. If they are a complete clause, use a semicolon.
Start with Bring one thing ___ a hat. Is a hat a complete clause?
items.explanation: Colons introduce a list or an explanation, such as a hat or the rain. Semicolons join two complete, closely linked clauses, such as Ayu sang and Dewi played the flute.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

options.text: The museum was closed; we visited the park instead.
The museum was closed, we visited the park instead.
options.why: A comma alone cannot join two complete clauses.

options.text: The museum was closed we visited the park instead.
options.why: Two complete clauses need punctuation or a joining word between them.

options.text: The museum; was closed we visited the park instead.
options.why: The semicolon is in the wrong place.

hints: There are two complete clauses in each sentence.
Two complete clauses can be joined with a semicolon, but not with a comma alone.
Find where the first clause ends.
items.explanation: A semicolon can join two complete clauses. Using only a comma is a mistake called a comma splice.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon to introduce an explanation?

options.text: Raka was soaked, he had forgotten his umbrella.
options.why: A comma alone cannot join two complete clauses.

options.text: Raka was soaked: he had forgotten his umbrella.
Raka: was soaked because he forgot his umbrella.
options.why: The colon separates the subject from its verb.

options.text: Raka was: soaked.
options.why: The colon breaks the clause in the middle.

hints: The second part of the sentence explains the first part.
A colon can come between a statement and its explanation.
Find the sentence with a complete clause on each side of the colon.
items.explanation: The second clause explains why Raka was soaked, so a colon can introduce it.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses semicolons correctly in a list?

options.text: We visited Bogor; which has a famous botanic garden, Bandung; which is cool and hilly, and Malang; which is known for its apples.
options.why: The semicolons should separate the whole items, not come in front of which.

options.text: We visited; Bogor, which has a famous botanic garden, Bandung, which is cool and hilly, and Malang, which is known for its apples.
options.why: A semicolon cannot come straight after visited.

options.text: We visited Bogor, which has a famous botanic garden; Bandung, which is cool and hilly; and Malang, which is known for its apples.
We visited Bogor, which has a famous botanic garden, Bandung, which is cool and hilly; and Malang; which is known for its apples.
options.why: The semicolons are in the wrong places.

hints: When list items already contain commas, semicolons separate the items.
Each item is a place plus some extra information about it.
Find the end of the Bogor item. What punctuation comes next?
items.explanation: Each item already has a comma inside it, so semicolons separate the three items clearly: Bogor; Bandung; and Malang.

items.prompt: Each item in this list contains a comma. How many semicolons are needed? The club has three leaders: Tia, who plans the games, Bayu, who looks after the money, and Kiki, who writes the newsletter.
hints: Semicolons go between the items of a list when the items already contain commas.
Find the three items first: each one is a name plus extra information.
Count the gaps between the three items.
items.explanation: Semicolons go after games and after money: Tia, who plans the games; Bayu, who looks after the money; and Kiki, who writes the newsletter.

items.prompt: Read: I have three hobbies: reading, swimming and painting; my sister has none. Why is there a semicolon after painting?

options.text: to introduce a list
options.why: The colon after hobbies introduces the list.

options.text: to show a pause in speech
options.why: Semicolons do not mark speech.

options.text: to separate the items in the list
options.why: Commas separate the items in this list.

options.text: to join two complete clauses that are closely linked

hints: Look at what comes before and after the semicolon.
My sister has none makes sense on its own.
Ask: is the first part a complete clause too?
items.explanation: I have three hobbies: reading, swimming and painting is a complete clause, and so is my sister has none. The semicolon links these two related clauses.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon correctly to introduce a list?
hints: A colon comes after a complete first part.
The list comes after the colon.
Find the sentence where Pack these things is a full statement before the mark.
items.explanation: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces what comes next, such as a list.

options.text: Pack: a torch, a map and a hat.
options.why: The words before a colon should make a full sentence. Pack on its own is too short.

options.text: Pack these things: a torch, a map and a hat.
Pack these things; a torch, a map and a hat.
options.why: A semicolon does not introduce a list. A colon does.

options.text: Pack these things, a torch: a map and a hat.
options.why: The colon is in the middle of the list. It belongs before the list.

items.prompt: Put the cards in order to make a sentence with a list.
hints: The colon comes after the first part of the sentence.
The words after the colon are a list.
Start with I bought.
items.explanation: The colon follows the complete clause I bought three things and introduces the list.
items.answer: I bought three things: milk, eggs and rice.

items.prompt: She had one rule ___ always be kind. Dewi loves swimming ___ her brother prefers running.
hints: The first gap introduces an explanation of the rule.
The second gap joins two related complete sentences.
A colon explains. A semicolon links.
items.explanation: A colon introduces the explanation of the rule. A semicolon joins two closely linked clauses.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
hints: A semicolon joins two parts that could each be a sentence.
Cover one side with your finger. Does the other side still make sense alone?
Look for the sentence where both halves can stand alone.
items.explanation: A semicolon joins two complete, related clauses. Both The sky grew dark and A storm was coming can stand alone.

options.text: The sky grew dark; because a storm was coming.
options.why: The part after a semicolon should be able to stand alone. Because a storm was coming cannot.

options.text: When the sky grew dark; we went inside.
options.why: The part before a semicolon should be able to stand alone. When the sky grew dark cannot.

options.text: The sky grew dark; a storm was coming.
The sky grew dark; and then.
options.why: The part after the semicolon is not a complete sentence.

items.prompt: Write the name of the punctuation mark that belongs in the gap. Kofi had one wish ___ to see the sea.
hints: The words after the gap explain the wish.
Which mark introduces an explanation?
It looks like two dots, one above the other.
items.explanation: The colon introduces an explanation of the wish.

items.prompt: Write the missing punctuation mark. The rain stopped ___ the sun came out.
hints: There are two complete sentences that belong together.
A full stop would separate them. Which mark joins them more gently?
It looks like a full stop with a comma under it.
items.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related clauses: The rain stopped; the sun came out.

items.prompt: Match each sentence to the job of its punctuation.
hints: Look at the mark and at what comes after it.
A list or explanation after a colon. Two full clauses with a semicolon.
Start with the sentence that has the semicolon.
items.explanation: Colons introduce lists and explanations. Semicolons join clauses that are closely related.
pairs: Bring these: a hat, a map and a torch.
I have one rule: be kind.
Rani sang; Bima played the drum.
The semicolon joins two related clauses

items.prompt: Put the cards in order to make a correct sentence.
hints: A semicolon joins two clauses that could be sentences.
The first clause is short.
Start with It was late.
items.explanation: It was late and The shops had already closed are two related sentences, joined by a semicolon.
items.answer: It was late; the shops had already closed.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
hints: Check what comes before each mark.
My favourite fruits are is not a full sentence on its own.
Try reading each version without the colon or semicolon.
items.explanation: Do not put a colon straight after a verb like are. The sentence is complete without a colon.

options.text: My favourite fruits are: mangoes, pineapples and bananas.
options.why: The words before a colon should be a complete sentence. Are cannot end one.

options.text: My favourite fruits: are mangoes, pineapples and bananas.
options.why: The colon is in the wrong place. It cuts the verb from its subject.

options.text: My favourite fruits are; mangoes, pineapples and bananas.
options.why: A semicolon should join two complete clauses. This one does not.

options.text: My favourite fruits are mangoes, pineapples and bananas.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences with correct punctuation.
hints: Check that the words before a colon make a full sentence.
Check that a semicolon has a complete clause on both sides.
Look at what follows each semicolon.
items.explanation: Each correct sentence has a full clause before the mark. Semicolons also need a full clause after them.

options.text: The trip had one rule: stay together.
Amara plays the piano; Tom plays the drums.
There are three planets I like: Mars, Venus and Saturn.
I like: apples, pears and plums.
options.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. I like is not complete.

options.text: We went to the park; and played football.
options.why: The part after the semicolon cannot stand alone.

options.text: Bayu was tired; because he ran.
options.why: The part after the semicolon cannot stand alone.

items.prompt: Write the two missing marks. The recipe needs three things ___ flour, eggs and milk ___ it is very simple.
hints: The first gap introduces a list.
The second gap joins two related clauses.
The first is a colon and the second is a semicolon.
items.explanation: A colon introduces the list and a semicolon joins the two related clauses.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated and worded correctly?
hints: Two full clauses are joined by however.
Which mark can join two full clauses, with however and a comma after it?
Check each sentence for extra words and for the mark before however.
items.explanation: A semicolon joins the two clauses, and however is followed by a comma.

options.text: Rani wanted to go swimming; because it was too cold.
options.why: The part after a semicolon should stand alone, and because makes it incomplete here.

options.text: Rani wanted to go swimming, but however, it was too cold.
options.why: But and however do the same job, so one is enough. A comma also cannot join full clauses with however.

options.text: Rani wanted to go swimming; however, it was too cold.
Rani wanted to go swimming: it was too cold, however.
options.why: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. It does not join contrasting clauses like this.

items.prompt: Which sentence punctuates this list best?
hints: Each item already has a comma inside it.
Use a stronger mark between whole items.
Group each town with its province.
items.explanation: When list items have commas inside, semicolons separate the items so the reader can see them clearly.

options.text: Our class visited Bogor, West Java, Malang, East Java and Medan, North Sumatra.
options.why: The commas make it hard to tell where one place ends and the next begins.

options.text: Our class visited: Bogor, West Java; Malang, East Java; and Medan, North Sumatra.
options.why: A colon should not follow a verb like visited.

options.text: Our class visited Bogor; West Java, Malang; East Java and Medan; North Sumatra.
options.why: The semicolons are in the wrong places. They split each place from its province.

options.text: Our class visited Bogor, West Java; Malang, East Java; and Medan, North Sumatra.

items.prompt: Put the cards in order to make a correct sentence.
hints: A semicolon joins two clauses.
However sits inside commas.
Start with Rani loves science.
items.explanation: The semicolon joins the clauses, and however is set off with commas.
items.answer: Rani loves science; her brother, however, prefers art.

items.prompt: Which sentence would be better with a semicolon instead of a colon?
hints: A colon explains or lists. A semicolon links two equal clauses.
Which sentence has two clauses that are equally important?
Check which sentence does not explain or list anything after the mark.
items.explanation: Dewi loves art and Wulan prefers music are equal, related clauses, so a semicolon suits them better.

options.text: Dewi loves art: Wulan prefers music.
She had one aim: to win.
options.why: The colon introduces what the aim is, so it is the correct mark.

options.text: Remember: bring your coat.
options.why: The colon introduces the thing to remember, so it is correct.

options.text: Pack three things: a hat, a coat and a map.
options.why: The colon introduces a list, so it is correct.
